summary.summary: Blaby's unaudited 2025/26 accounts show a financially healthy district: the year ended £1.6m better than budget (a £1,613,572 surplus where the Q3 forecast was a £240,689 drawdown from balances), lifting the general fund balance to £8.262m — 43.0% of the 2026/27 net budget requirement, just under the council's own 45% ceiling — with earmarked reserves up £4.0m to £15.6m. Debt is minimal and falling: £4.0m of PWLB loans at 2.08% against a £21.6m capital financing requirement, the £17.6m gap run as internal borrowing (using own cash instead of loans), alongside £19.6m of short-term investments. Behind the good headline sit three watch items: the business-rates collection fund swung from a £2.3m surplus to a £2.7m deficit (Blaby's £1.1m share lands in the 2027/28 budget, and the national business-rates reset 'heavily reduces' retained rates from 2026/27); a residual £0.745m sits in the UBS Triton property fund pending recovery from the terminated Lothbury fund; and a prior-year IFRS 16 leasing error (liabilities understated) was corrected while the pension liability rose from £7.3m to £11.6m.

signals.headline: Unaudited 2025/26 accounts signed and published by 30 June 2026; auditor Azets will not start the audit until September 2026, with 2024/25 accounts published at the 27 February 2026 backstop
signals.why: Preparation is on time and the outturn is favourable, but the figures remain unassured until the autumn audit concludes.

signals.headline: PWLB debt fell from £4.858m to £4.000m during 2025/26 (average rate 2.08%), with the £21.558m CFR internally borrowed by £17.558m and £19.6m of short-term investments on hand
signals.why: External debt is trivial relative to reserves and investments, so lender exposure to Blaby is small and shrinking.

news_drafts.headline: Blaby council raises capital spending plan by 69% to £8.5m, with most projects still unstarted
news_drafts.lead: Blaby council has increased its capital programme—money for buildings, roads and equipment—from £5.1m to £8.5m for 2026/27, a rise driven largely by bringing forward £3.4m of unspent budgets from the previous year. The council approved borrowing of £3.77m to fund the enlarged programme. However, the council had deployed only £1.2m of the £8.5m budget by the end of June, three months in. The largest project, a £4.5m regeneration property scheme, was 78 per cent unspent. Other schemes including fleet vehicle replacement (£671k) and IT infrastructure improvements (£125k) had spent nothing. The council said it is reviewing its disabled facilities grants service provider to improve delivery. The UK Shared Prosperity Fund, by contrast, spent 99 per cent of its budget in the same period, suggesting the council can execute capital programmes rapidly when actively managed.
news_drafts.paper_title: Appendix D – Treasury and Prudential Indicators

news_drafts.headline: Blaby approves £8.5m capital programme but deploys just 14% in first quarter
news_drafts.lead: Blaby Council has approved a revised capital programme of £8.5m for 2026/27, a 69% increase on its original £5.1m budget, but has spent only £1.2m by the end of June. The largest project, a £4.5m regeneration property scheme, remains 78% unspent. Multiple capital projects, including the Walk & Ride Blaby scheme and fleet vehicle replacement programme, have not begun. The council has approved £3.77m of prudential borrowing—new internal borrowing to fund the expanded programme—representing a 44% increase on the original borrowing requirement. One exception is the UK Shared Prosperity Fund, which deployed 99% of its budget in the quarter, suggesting the council can execute rapidly when programmes are actively managed.

findings.paper_title: Recommendations of the Cabinet Executive: Quarter 1 Treasury Management Update 2026/27 Report
findings.headline: Investment income on track with elevated rates supporting Q1 performance
findings.detail: The council's investment income performance is tracking to budget with elevated market rates during Q1 2026/27. By 30 June 2026, the council had secured £0.251m against its full-year budget of £1.1m. Officers confirm that approved investment limits were not breached and continue to monitor counterparty creditworthiness.
findings.matters: Shows council is capturing budgeted investment returns and maintaining investment discipline
findings.figures: 2026/27 investment income budget: £1.1m; secured to 30 June: £0.251m; funds available for investment: £25.9m
findings.quote: The Council's budget for in-house investment income in 2026/27 is £1.1m. On 30th June, the Council had secured a return of £0.251m.

findings.paper_title: Recommendations of the Cabinet Executive: Quarter 1 Treasury Management Update 2026/27 Report
findings.headline: Council relies on internal borrowing to fund capital; reserves will require future replenishment
findings.detail: The council has been in an internally borrowed cash position for several years, funding capital schemes from reserves rather than external borrowing. Officers plan to maintain this strategy while investment rates remain lower than borrowing rates, but balances will need replenishing subject to expenditure demands. Officers closely monitor reserves, balances and cashflows supporting this position.
findings.matters: Shows council's capital funding depends on finite reserve depletion; future spending will require either external borrowing or reserve rebuilding
findings.figures: External debt (excluding Finance Leases) £4m at 30 June 2026; funds available for investment £25.9m
findings.quote: For several years, the Council has been in an internally borrowed cash position, and balances will need to be replenished at some point in the future, subject to expenditure demands.

findings.paper_title: Recommendations of the Cabinet Executive: Quarter 1 Treasury Management Update 2026/27 Report
findings.headline: Council increases borrowing limits after correcting prior-year IFRS 16 treatment of finance lease
findings.detail: An error in implementing IFRS 16 on a finance lease in 2024/25 was identified during the audit and has been corrected with specialist advice. As a result, if the council were to borrow externally for all approved capital schemes, it would exceed existing prudential limits. The council therefore proposes to increase Operational Boundary from £20.7m to £22.224m and Authorised Limit from £23m to £25.3m.
findings.matters: Reveals accounting restatement, shows extent of council's committed capital spending, and increases approved debt capacity
findings.figures: Operational Boundary: £20,700,000 to £22,224,000; Authorised Limit: £23,000,000 to £25,300,000
findings.quote: Following the Audit of the Financial Accounts for 2024/25, Officers became aware of an error in the way in which IFRS16 was implemented on a finance lease in 2024/25.

findings.headline: Regular public sector pay growth accelerated to 5.1% three-monthly year-on-year, up from 4.8%
findings.detail: While private sector pay growth has eased to 3.4% excluding bonuses, regular public sector pay growth accelerated from 4.8% to 5.1% three-monthly year-on-year. This means council payroll costs are growing significantly faster than CPI inflation of 2.8%, creating sustained budget pressure across local authorities.
findings.matters: Payroll typically represents 60-70% of council spending; pay growth outpacing inflation creates budget pressure
findings.figures: Public sector pay 5.1% vs private sector 3.4% (ex-bonus) vs CPI 2.8%
findings.quote: regular public sector pay growth accelerated from 4.8% 3myy to 5.1% 3myy.

findings.headline: Public sector net borrowing £23.3bn in May, £5.4bn above May 2025 and above OBR forecast
findings.detail: Government borrowing in May reached £23.3bn, £5.4bn higher than May 2025 and above the OBR's forecast of £17.7bn. Debt interest payments hit £4.1bn above May 2025 (the highest in any May on record) and £3.3bn above OBR prediction. Government borrowing forecast to rise from 4.2% of GDP in 2025/26 to 4.4% in 2026/27, reflecting fiscal pressure affecting market conditions for local authority borrowing.
findings.matters: Higher government borrowing affects gilt market conditions and availability of funding for local authorities
findings.figures: £23.3bn (vs £17.7bn forecast), £5.4bn above May 2025, borrowing forecast rising to 4.4% from 4.2% of GDP
findings.quote: Public sector net borrowing of £23.3bn in May was above the OBR's forecast of £17.7bn and £5.4bn above May's figure last year.
